title: The Ellis and Baldwin test of the Cosmic Dipole: Exploring the impact of multiple flux density cuts
comment: 26 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP)
summary: The cosmic dipole tension - the discrepancy between the Cosmic Microwave Background kinematic dipole and the matter dipole inferred from all-sky surveys poses a significant challenge to the Cosmological Principle, which dictates that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic at the largest scales. Traditional measurement of the matter dipole requires selecting an appropriate limiting flux and calculating the dipolar modulation using sources brighter than the flux. This approach, however, ignores the shape of the source luminosity function (LF) and deprives the analysis of this crucial information. In this study, we present a new approach to calculate the matter dipole by integrating the source flux distribution into the analysis. We achieve this by dividing the catalogue into disjoint flux bins and simultaneously fitting the matter dipole across them. For non-power-law LFs, this method gives a higher Bayes factor - and hence a better description of the matter dipole - as compared to the traditional approach. The method works best when the flux cuts are selected in regions where the LF's shape changes significantly. We discuss the feasibility of this method for upcoming cosmological surveys and show that it has the potential to yield decisive results at both radio and infrared wavelengths.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new method for measuring the cosmic matter dipole by incorporating source luminosity function information through flux-binned analysis, offering improved sensitivity compared to traditional flux-cut approaches, especially for non-power-law luminosity functions.
AI.motivation: The cosmic dipole tension challenges the Cosmological Principle. Traditional matter dipole measurements use a single flux cut, ignoring the shape of the source luminosity function. This study aims to incorporate LF information to improve dipole estimation and potentially resolve the tension.
AI.method: Instead of a single flux cut, the authors divide the catalogue into disjoint flux bins and simultaneously fit the matter dipole across all bins. This integrates the source flux distribution (luminosity function shape) into the analysis. Bayesian model comparison is used to evaluate performance.
AI.result: For non-power-law LFs, the new method yields a higher Bayes factor (better description of the matter dipole) than the traditional approach. The method performs best when flux cuts target regions where the LF shape changes significantly.
AI.conclusion: The method is feasible for upcoming cosmological surveys and has the potential to deliver decisive results on the dipole tension at both radio and infrared wavelengths.

title: GINKAKU: Scalable Cosmological Structure Formation Simulation Code and Post-processing Pipeline
summary: We introduce GINKAKU, a new cosmological $N$-body code developed for the Dark Quest II (DQ2) simulation campaign and designed for controlled ensemble production across the cosmological model space required by next-generation galaxy surveys, including massive neutrinos and clustering dark energy. Built on the FDPS framework, GINKAKU couples a TreePM gravity solver with a linear-response treatment of external source terms for components not evolved as $N$-body particles, formulated in the $N$-body gauge. This design incorporates massive-neutrino perturbations, general-relativistic corrections, early-time radiation perturbations, and dark-energy clustering with non-unit effective sound speed at the linear level, while preserving Newtonian particle dynamics on subhorizon scales. The code is validated through internal convergence studies and cross-comparisons with GADGET, PKDGRAV3, and RAMSES on shared initial conditions: code-to-code differences in the nonlinear power spectrum can be reduced below $\sim1\%$ level by tuning internal accuracy parameters, and we identify a production-grade fiducial setting achieving this control at modest cost. We apply GINKAKU to an initial set of DQ2 production runs -- eight cosmological models with $3,000^3$ particles in boxes up to $4\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Gpc}$ -- processed by a renewed post-processing pipeline that reduces the inter-resolution spread of the halo mass function to $\sim 1\%$ and includes halo-shape measurements for intrinsic-alignment statistics. The scale-dependent-growth cosmologies reproduce the expected nonlinear signatures of massive neutrinos and clustering dark energy, demonstrating suitability for emulator-scale production. A total matter power spectrum emulator from these runs is presented in an accompanying paper. (abridged)

AI.tldr: GINKAKU is a new cosmological N-body code built on the FDPS framework with a TreePM gravity solver and linear-response treatment for massive neutrinos, GR corrections, radiation perturbations, and clustering dark energy. It achieves <1% cross-code agreement with GADGET, PKDGRAV3, and RAMSES, and is used for the Dark Quest II campaign with 3,000³ particles in up to 4 h⁻¹ Gpc boxes, including halo shape measurements and a power spectrum emulator.
AI.motivation: To develop a cosmological N-body code capable of controlled ensemble production across the model space required by next-generation galaxy surveys, incorporating massive neutrinos, clustering dark energy, and general-relativistic corrections while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: Built on FDPS framework, GINKAKU couples a TreePM gravity solver with a linear-response treatment of external source terms in the N-body gauge. Massive-neutrino perturbations, GR corrections, early-time radiation perturbations, and dark-energy clustering with non-unit effective sound speed are included at linear level while preserving Newtonian particle dynamics on subhorizon scales. A renewed post-processing pipeline reduces halo mass function inter-resolution spread to ~1% and includes halo-shape measurements.
AI.result: Code-to-code differences in the nonlinear power spectrum can be reduced below ~1% with tuned accuracy parameters. Production runs with eight cosmological models, 3,000³ particles in boxes up to 4 h⁻¹ Gpc, show expected nonlinear signatures of massive neutrinos and clustering dark energy. A total matter power spectrum emulator has been produced.
AI.conclusion: GINKAKU demonstrates suitability for emulator-scale production across cosmological model space, enabling the Dark Quest II simulation campaign for next-generation galaxy surveys.

title: Dark Quest II: A Wide-Coverage Neural Network Emulator of the Nonlinear Matter Power Spectrum Across Extended Cosmologies
comment: 53 pages, 44 figures, emulator code available at https://github.com/DarkQuestCosmology/dark_emulator2_public
summary: \textsc{DarkEmulator2} is a neural network emulator of the nonlinear matter power spectrum in a nine-dimensional $w_0 w_a νo \mathrm{CDM}$ parameter space, developed as the emulator component of the \textsc{Dark Quest II} (DQ2) program. It is trained on simulations generated with the \textsc{Ginkaku} code, whose numerical implementation, accuracy tests, and post-processing pipeline are described in the companion paper. The design follows a unified strategy: in addition to the cosmological parameter vector, we supplement the neural network's inputs with three families of physically motivated auxiliary quantities -- the linear matter power spectrum, descriptors of the simulation resolution, and a low-dimensional summary of the initial Gaussian random field -- that are expected to improve generalization across the parameter space. Training a single network jointly across three simulation resolution tiers allows the emulator to exploit a small number of high-resolution simulations while retaining broad coverage from lower-resolution simulations. For a $L_{\mathrm{box}}=1\,\hiGpc$ box with $N=3000^{3}$ particles, the emulator reproduces the simulated matter power spectrum to subpercent accuracy up to the particle Nyquist scale, $k_{\mathrm{Ny}}\simeq 10\,\hMpci$. The emulator remains accurate over the calibrated wavenumber range, while its highest-$k$ predictions depend on the simulation resolution and shot noise. We validate the emulator on independent test suites and, through a cross-comparison with several public emulators and widely used fitting formulas, characterize the inter-model consistency and the parameter-dependent trends in their residuals.

AI.tldr: DarkEmulator2 is a neural network emulator for the nonlinear matter power spectrum across a nine-dimensional cosmological parameter space, trained on simulations from the Ginkaku code. It uses physically motivated auxiliary inputs (linear power spectrum, resolution descriptors, initial field summaries) and joint training across three resolution tiers to achieve subpercent accuracy up to the Nyquist scale, validated against independent tests and compared with other public emulators.
AI.motivation: To develop a fast and accurate emulator for the nonlinear matter power spectrum over a broad nine-dimensional cosmological parameter space, improving generalization by incorporating physically motivated auxiliary inputs and leveraging multi-resolution simulation training.
AI.method: A neural network emulator trained on Ginkaku N-body simulations. The input includes cosmological parameters plus three families of auxiliary quantities: linear matter power spectrum, simulation resolution descriptors, and a low-dimensional summary of the initial Gaussian random field. Joint training across three resolution tiers is employed to combine high-resolution accuracy with broad low-resolution coverage.
AI.result: Subpercent accuracy up to the particle Nyquist scale (k_Ny ≈ 10 h/Mpc) for a L_box=1 h⁻¹Gpc box with N=3000³ particles. Accuracy degrades beyond the calibrated range and is resolution- and shot-noise-dependent. Validated on independent test suites and cross-compared with other emulators and fitting formulas.
AI.conclusion: The unified auxiliary-input strategy and multi-resolution joint training yield a robust and accurate emulator. Cross-comparisons reveal inter-model consistency and parameter-dependent trends in residuals, establishing DarkEmulator2 as a reliable component of the Dark Quest II program.

title: Exploring non-Poisson satellite occupation in HOD models and its impact on 2- and 3-point galaxy clustering
summary: Understanding the connection between galaxies and dark matter halos is a central challenge in modern cosmology. The Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) framework provides a widely used statistical description of how galaxies populate dark matter halos, enabling precise modelling of galaxy clustering. A common assumption in standard HOD models is that the number of satellite galaxies follows a Poisson distribution at fixed halo mass. In this work, we revisit this assumption and introduce the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) distribution as a minimal extension of of the Poisson model, which add a single parameter, $ν$, to explore sub- and super-Poisson behaviour. We derive analytical approximations for the CMP expectation parameter $λ$ and develop a numerical scheme that smoothly connects small- and large-$λ$ regimes, achieving $\sim5\%$ accuracy for $0.5 < ν< 2$. Using the \texttt{HODDIES} package, we study the impact of non-Poisson satellite occupations on mock galaxy catalogues and clustering statistics. Variations in the variance of the satellite occupation significantly affect small-scale clustering, producing deviations of up to $10\%$ in projected clustering and $5\%$ in the monopole and quadrupole. We further investigate higher-order statistics using counts-in-cylinders (CiC) and the tree-level galaxy bispectrum. CiC statistics are highly sensitive to changes in the variance, with variations up to $\sim30\%$, while the tree-level galaxy bispectrum (in the Sugiyama basis) is only weakly affected ($<2\%$ up to $k_\mathrm{max} = 0.3$). These results suggest that non-Poisson satellite statistics are important for small-scale analyses, but should have a limited impact on cosmological constraints from power spectrum and bispectrum measurements using large scales $k_\mathrm{max} < 0.3$.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) distribution as a minimal extension to standard HOD models, allowing for sub- and super-Poisson satellite galaxy occupations. The CMP model achieves ~5% accuracy for ν between 0.5 and 2. Non-Poisson satellite statistics significantly affect small-scale clustering (up to 10% in projected clustering) and counts-in-cylinders (~30% variation), but have limited impact (<2%) on the galaxy bispectrum and power spectrum at large scales (k_max < 0.3).
AI.motivation: To revisit the common assumption that satellite galaxy numbers follow a Poisson distribution at fixed halo mass in HOD models, and to explore whether non-Poisson behavior impacts galaxy clustering and higher-order statistics.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) distribution as a one-parameter (ν) extension to model sub- and super-Poisson satellite occupations. They derive analytical approximations for the CMP expectation parameter λ, develop a numerical scheme for smooth interpolation between small- and large-λ regimes, and use the HODDIES package to generate mock catalogues and compute clustering statistics including projected clustering, monopole/quadrupole, counts-in-cylinders (CiC), and tree-level galaxy bispectrum.
AI.result: The CMP model achieves ~5% accuracy for 0.5 < ν < 2. Non-Poisson satellite variance causes up to 10% deviations in projected clustering, 5% in monopole/quadrupole, ~30% in counts-in-cylinders, but <2% in the tree-level galaxy bispectrum (Sugiyama basis) up to k_max = 0.3.
AI.conclusion: Non-Poisson satellite statistics are important for small-scale analyses but should have limited impact on cosmological constraints from power spectrum and bispectrum measurements using large scales (k_max < 0.3).

title: Measuring the Hubble constant with strongly lensed gravitational waves from space-based detector networks
summary: The measurement of the Hubble constant $H_0$ plays a central role in modern cosmology. In this work, we investigate the potential of strongly lensed gravitational-wave (SLGW) signals from massive binary black hole mergers to constrain $H_0$ using future space-based detector networks. We consider two observational scenarios: one in which the source redshift is unknown, and another in which it is independently determined through electromagnetic observations. We show that meaningful constraints on $H_0$ can still be achieved without source-redshift information, provided that the lens redshift is known. For individual SLGW events, the joint Taiji+LISA analysis improves the measurement precision of $H_0$ by approximately a factor of two compared with the Taiji-only configuration. Extending the analysis to the population level, we combine five simulated SLGW events and find that the uncertainty in $H_0$, quantified by the 95\% credible interval, reaches the $1.1\times10^{-1}$ level when the source redshift is treated as unknown, and further improves to $4.2\times10^{-2}$ when the source redshift is independently measured. Our results demonstrate that joint space-based gravitational-wave observations can substantially enhance the cosmological capability of SLGW events and provide a promising avenue for precision measurements of the Hubble constant.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using strongly lensed gravitational-wave signals from binary black hole mergers, observed by future space-based detectors (Taiji+LISA), to constrain the Hubble constant $H_0$, showing that meaningful constraints are achievable even without source redshift knowledge, and precision improves significantly with population-level analysis and independent redshift measurements.
AI.motivation: The Hubble constant $H_0$ is central to modern cosmology, and the authors aim to investigate whether strongly lensed gravitational-wave signals from massive binary black hole mergers can serve as a new, independent probe to constrain $H_0$, especially using future space-based detector networks.
AI.method: The authors consider two observational scenarios: (1) source redshift unknown, lens redshift known; (2) source redshift independently determined via electromagnetic observations. They quantify $H_0$ measurement precision using individual events (Taiji-only vs. joint Taiji+LISA) and extend to a population-level analysis combining five simulated SLGW events, reporting 95% credible intervals.
AI.result: For individual events, joint Taiji+LISA improves $H_0$ precision by ~2× over Taiji-only. At the population level (5 events), the 95% credible interval on $H_0$ reaches $1.1\times10^{-1}$ (source redshift unknown) and improves to $4.2\times10^{-2}$ (source redshift independently measured).
AI.conclusion: Joint space-based gravitational-wave observations can substantially enhance the cosmological capability of SLGW events and provide a promising avenue for precision measurements of the Hubble constant.

title: Testing cosmic anisotropy with the Combo correlation of gamma-ray bursts
summary: We employ the sample of 244 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs; i.e., C244) with the Combo correlation to test cosmic anisotropy. Meanwhile, the Pantheon sample is introduced to verify whether the GRB sample can suppress the fake anisotropic signals induced by inhomogeneous spatial distributions. In the dipole fitting (DF) method, under the dipole-modulated $Λ$CDM model, the C244 sample shifts the best-fitting longitude $l$ derived from the Pantheon sample by $54.09^\circ$ and reduces the uncertainty in $l$ by approximately $40\%$. Compared to the 118 GRBs (i.e., A118) with the $E_\mathrm{p}$-$E_\mathrm{iso}$ correlation, the shift in longitude $l$ increases by additional $21.35^\circ$. In the hemisphere comparison (HC) method, the preferred direction derived from the C244+Pantheon sample deviates from that of the Pantheon-only sample by more than $1σ$. In contrast, the preferred direction from the A118+Pantheon sample is consistent with the Pantheon-only result within the $1σ$ uncertainty. The preferred direction changes significantly as the number of GRBs increases from 118 to 244. Our results show that a larger GRB sample can reduce the fake anisotropic signals caused by inhomogeneous spatial distributions. Accordingly, we suggest that GRBs have the potential to provide a reliable probe of cosmic anisotropy.

AI.tldr: Using 244 GRBs with the Combo correlation and the Pantheon sample, the study finds that larger GRB samples can reduce fake anisotropic signals from inhomogeneous spatial distributions, suggesting GRBs can reliably probe cosmic anisotropy.
AI.motivation: To test cosmic anisotropy and verify whether the GRB sample can suppress fake anisotropic signals induced by inhomogeneous spatial distributions.
AI.method: Applied dipole fitting (DF) under the dipole-modulated ΛCDM model and hemisphere comparison (HC) method to C244 (Combo correlation) and A118 (Ep-Eiso correlation) GRB samples, combined with the Pantheon sample.
AI.result: C244 shifts the best-fitting longitude by 54.09° and reduces uncertainty by ~40% relative to Pantheon alone; A118 shifts by additional 21.35°. HC shows C244+Pantheon deviates >1σ from Pantheon-only, while A118+Pantheon is consistent within 1σ. Preferred direction changes significantly as GRB count increases from 118 to 244.
AI.conclusion: A larger GRB sample (C244) reduces fake anisotropic signals more effectively than a smaller one (A118), indicating GRBs can provide a reliable probe of cosmic anisotropy.

title: Entropic backreaction from cosmic structure formation: a thermodynamic approach to the late-time cosmological tensions
summary: High-precision cosmological observations have revealed persistent tensions within the standard $Λ$CDM paradigm, most notably the discrepancy in the Hubble constant and the lower than predicted amplitude of late-time matter clustering quantified by $S_8$. We propose a unified thermodynamic framework in which entropic backreaction generated during cosmic structure formation modifies both the background expansion history and the growth of matter perturbations. As gravitational instability drives the growth of cosmic structures, the configuration entropy associated with the matter distribution decreases through the nonlinear redistribution of gravitational binding energy. The resulting entropic energy density contributes a late-time backreaction that enhances the cosmic expansion rate without altering early-Universe physics or the CMB sound horizon. Simultaneously, the same irreversible entropy dissipation process induces a dissipative correction within the cosmic velocity flow, suppressing the efficiency of coherent gravitational clustering at late times. The framework operates entirely within standard General Relativity: the Einstein field equations, Poisson equation, and gravitational coupling remain unmodified, and no new propagating degrees of freedom or fifth forces are introduced. Entropic backreaction therefore provides a thermodynamically motivated, theoretically conservative, and observationally testable mechanism that may simultaneously alleviate the major late-time cosmological tensions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified thermodynamic framework where entropic backreaction from cosmic structure formation simultaneously resolves the Hubble tension and the S8 tension by modifying the expansion history and suppressing late-time clustering, all within standard General Relativity without new degrees of freedom.
AI.motivation: Persistent tensions within the ΛCDM paradigm—the Hubble constant discrepancy and the lower-than-expected S8 amplitude—motivate a mechanism that addresses both without altering early-Universe physics or introducing new forces.
AI.method: A thermodynamic framework where configuration entropy decrease during gravitational structure formation generates an entropic energy density that backreacts on the background expansion, while irreversible entropy dissipation introduces a dissipative correction to the cosmic velocity flow, suppressing late-time clustering.
AI.result: Entropic backreaction enhances the late-time expansion rate (alleviating the H0 tension) and simultaneously suppresses coherent gravitational clustering (alleviating the S8 tension), all without modifying Einstein field equations, Poisson equation, or gravitational coupling, and without introducing new degrees of freedom or fifth forces.
AI.conclusion: Entropic backreaction offers a thermodynamically motivated, theoretically conservative, and observationally testable mechanism that may simultaneously alleviate the major late-time cosmological tensions within standard General Relativity.

title: Whispers of Supergravity in Gravitational Wave Backgrounds: Determining the Gravitino Mass from Cosmic Thermal History
summary: Gravitino masses above the electroweak scale provide the simplest solution to the gravitino problem, but such large mass scales lie far beyond the reach of collider experiments. We show that the stochastic gravitational wave background offers a direct probe of this otherwise inaccessible regime. Despite decaying before Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN), these gravitinos naturally generate a period of early matter domination in the early universe. This non-standard epoch leaves a characteristic imprint on any primordial gravitational wave background, characterised by two frequencies corresponding to the onset and end of this phase. We demonstrate that these features can be used to directly infer both the gravitino mass and its initial abundance in a direct mapping. Future gravitational wave observatories span a vast frequency range, enabling sensitivity to gravitino masses from the BBN bound of $\mathcal{O}(100)\,\text{TeV}$ all the way up to $\mathcal{O}(10^{10})\,\text{TeV}$, with recent signal by NANOGrav already probing masses in the range $500$-$10^4$ TeV. Gravitational wave observables therefore probe an enormous region of parameter space, far beyond the reach of collider experiments. We are entering an era in which supergravity can be probed through gravitational wave backgrounds alongside collider experiments.

AI.tldr: Gravitino masses above the electroweak scale, inaccessible to colliders, can be directly probed through the stochastic gravitational wave background. The gravitino-induced early matter domination leaves characteristic imprints on gravitational waves, allowing inference of both mass and abundance. Future observatories can probe masses from ~100 TeV to 10^10 TeV, with NANOGrav already probing 500-10^4 TeV.
AI.motivation: Gravitinos with masses above the electroweak scale evade collider experiments but suffer from the gravitino problem. The authors aim to find a way to probe this otherwise inaccessible high-mass regime.
AI.method: The authors analyze how decaying gravitinos (before BBN) induce an early matter-dominated era, which imprints characteristic two-frequency features on any primordial stochastic gravitational wave background. From these features, the gravitino mass and initial abundance can be directly inferred.
AI.result: Future gravitational wave observatories can probe gravitino masses from ~100 TeV (BBN bound) up to ~10^10 TeV. NANOGrav already constrains masses in the 500-10^4 TeV range.
AI.conclusion: Gravitational wave observations can probe supergravity parameter space far beyond collider reach, marking a new era where supergravity is testable via gravitational wave backgrounds.

title: Fewer simulations, sharper covariances: Reducing mock covariance noise with Zeldovich approximation control variates
summary: We present a control-variate method for reducing the variance of power spectrum covariance matrix estimates from simulations of large-scale structure. The key idea is to pair each mock simulation with a cheap Zeldovich-approximation realization sharing the same initial conditions, and to use the known statistical properties of the Zeldovich field to remove correlated sample variance from the covariance estimator. Under a Gaussian disconnected approximation, we derive fully analytic expressions for both the optimal control-variate coefficient, $β(k,\ell;k',\ell')$, and the corresponding correlation, $ρ(k,\ell;k',\ell')$, in terms of the auto- and cross-power spectra of the target and control fields. In the monopole case, the correlation takes the particularly simple form $ρ(k,k') = r^2(k),r^2(k')$, where $r(k)$ is the standard cross-correlation coefficient between the target and Zeldovich fields, implying that covariance estimation remains highly efficient whenever the two fields are strongly correlated. For masked redshift-space lognormal mocks, resembling Luminous Red Galaxies from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), we find that the control-variate estimator reduces the variance of the covariance matrix by approximately an order of magnitude on large scales, $k \lesssim 0.05\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, precisely where accurate covariance estimation is most challenging. The gains are smaller for higher $k$ but typically accelerate convergence by a factor of 2-3, substantially lowering the computational cost of covariance estimation for current and upcoming large-scale structure surveys. Due to its simplicity, this method is readily implementable in current imaging and spectroscopic surveys (e.g., DESI, Euclid, LSST, PFS, SPHEREx).

AI.tldr: The paper presents a control-variate method using Zeldovich-approximation realizations to reduce variance in power spectrum covariance matrix estimates from large-scale structure simulations. It derives analytic expressions for optimal coefficients and correlations, showing order-of-magnitude variance reduction on large scales (k≲0.05 h Mpc⁻¹) and 2-3× acceleration at higher k, making it readily applicable to current and upcoming surveys like DESI, Euclid, LSST, PFS, and SPHEREx.
AI.motivation: Power spectrum covariance matrix estimation from simulations suffers from high sample variance, especially on large scales where accurate covariance estimation is most challenging. The computational cost of running enough mock simulations to achieve precise covariance estimates is prohibitive for current and upcoming large-scale structure surveys.
AI.method: The method pairs each mock simulation with a cheap Zeldovich-approximation realization sharing identical initial conditions. Using known statistical properties of the Zeldovich field, it removes correlated sample variance from the covariance estimator via a control-variate approach. Under a Gaussian disconnected approximation, analytic expressions are derived for the optimal control-variate coefficient β(k,ℓ;k',ℓ') and correlation ρ(k,ℓ;k',ℓ') in terms of auto- and cross-power spectra of the target and control fields.
AI.result: For masked redshift-space lognormal mocks resembling DESI LRGs, the control-variate estimator reduces covariance matrix variance by ~10× on large scales (k≲0.05 h Mpc⁻¹) and accelerates convergence by a factor of 2-3 at higher k. The monopole correlation takes the simple form ρ(k,k')=r²(k)r²(k'), where r(k) is the cross-correlation coefficient between target and Zeldovich fields.
AI.conclusion: The method substantially lowers the computational cost of covariance estimation and is readily implementable in current and upcoming large-scale structure surveys including DESI, Euclid, LSST, PFS, and SPHEREx.

title: Reconstructing the Globular Cluster Initial Mass Function from Present-Day Globular Cluster Systems
comment: Submitted to AAS Journals. 14 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Comments welcome
summary: The near-universal turnover mass of the present-day globular cluster mass function (GCMF), $M_{\rm TO} \sim 2 \times 10^5\ {\rm M_\odot}$, is a well established observational feature across galaxies of different types and masses, providing an important empirical benchmark for understanding the globular cluster initial mass function (GCIMF). Competing explanations of this property invoke either dynamical evolution from an initial power-law distribution or an imprint of cluster formation physics. We address this problem by reconstructing the high-mass regime of the GCIMF by inverting the mass loss due to dynamical evolution of present-day globular cluster systems across a wide range of host galaxy masses. Our method is based on an environment-dependent mass-loss model calibrated by direct $N$-body simulations in time-dependent tidal fields, enabling a mapping between observed cluster masses and their progenitor values without assuming a priori a functional form for the GCIMF. We apply our method to galaxies spanning halo masses of $\sim10^{9}$ - $10^{12}\ {\rm M_\odot}$, combining systems with individually measured globular cluster masses as well as large statistical samples constructed from observed global properties. The recovered GCIMFs are systematically shifted towards higher masses and exhibit a power-law behavior at the high-mass end. The inferred slopes vary across galaxies and show a strong correlation with host halo mass, with more massive galaxies exhibiting steeper high-mass slopes. Our results suggest that the slope of the GCIMF depends on the galactic properties and provides a direct empirical link between present-day globular cluster systems and their high-redshift progenitors.

AI.tldr: This paper reconstructs the high-mass regime of the globular cluster initial mass function (GCIMF) by inverting dynamical mass loss from present-day globular cluster systems across a wide range of host galaxy masses (halo masses ~10⁹–10¹² M☉). Using environment-dependent mass-loss models calibrated by N-body simulations, the authors find that recovered GCIMFs are power-law at high masses, with slopes that strongly correlate with host halo mass — more massive galaxies have steeper slopes — providing a direct empirical link between present-day GC systems and their high-redshift progenitors.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing debate about whether the near-universal turnover mass (~2×10⁵ M☉) in present-day globular cluster mass functions is due to dynamical evolution from an initial power-law distribution or an imprint of cluster formation physics.
AI.method: The authors invert dynamical mass loss using an environment-dependent mass-loss model calibrated by direct N-body simulations in time-dependent tidal fields. This allows mapping observed cluster masses to their progenitor values without assuming a functional form for the GCIMF. They apply this to galaxies spanning halo masses ~10⁹–10¹² M☉, combining individually measured GC masses and large statistical samples.
AI.result: Recovered GCIMFs are systematically shifted toward higher masses and exhibit power-law behavior at the high-mass end. Slopes vary across galaxies and strongly correlate with host halo mass: more massive galaxies have steeper high-mass slopes, indicating that the GCIMF slope depends on galactic properties.
AI.conclusion: The GCIMF slope depends on host galaxy properties, providing a direct empirical link between present-day globular cluster systems and their high-redshift progenitors, supporting the dynamical evolution scenario for shaping the observed GCMF turnover.

title: Resolving galaxy formation in the early Universe with BonFIRE and CampFIRE
comment: 43 pages, 21 figures, submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome
summary: The abundance and rapid growth of galaxies at cosmic dawn revealed by the James Webb Space Telescope challenges models of galaxy formation, motivating new simulations to uncover the processes driving early galaxy assembly. We present the first results from BonFIRE ($L\approx40$ cMpc, $m_{\rm baryon}\approx5\times10^4~\rm{M}_{\odot}$) and CampFIRE ($L\approx5$ cMpc, at both $m_{\rm baryon}\approx800~\rm{M}_{\odot}$ and $\approx6\times10^3~\rm{M}_{\odot}$), a suite of cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of early galaxy formation ($z\gtrsim6$) from the Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) project, using the FIRE-3 model. We use a resampling procedure to combine the large statistics of BonFIRE with the higher resolution of CampFIRE and robustly predict galaxy properties over a wide dynamic range ($M_{\star}\sim10^4-10^{10}~\rm{M}_{\odot}$). Galaxy formation in this suite emerges through clustered, bursty star formation, with halo-scale star formation efficiencies reaching $10-30\%$ in high-mass halos. A subset of low-mass halos also have surprisingly high efficiencies of $\gtrsim1\%$ and host ultra-compact galaxies with narrow age spreads. We predict galaxy UV luminosity functions at $9\lesssim~z\lesssim25$ in broad agreement with observations at $M_{\rm UV}\gtrsim-19$, with a faint-end turnover at $M_{\rm UV}\approx-14$, but we slightly overpredict the abundance of brighter galaxies. We find that UV luminosity variability in early galaxies is strongly mass-dependent, with halo-to-halo scatter dominating at low masses and contributing comparably to rapid temporal burstiness at $M_{\rm halo}\gtrsim10^{10}~\rm{M}_{\odot}$. We also present first results from a simple Pop~III model with a top-heavy IMF, demonstrating broad agreement with independent Pop~III predictions and observational constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper presents first results from the BonFIRE and CampFIRE simulations—a suite of high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamic simulations within the FIRE project—to study early galaxy formation at z≳6. By combining large statistics and high resolution via resampling, the simulations predict galaxy properties over a wide mass range (M⋆ ∼ 10⁴–10¹⁰ M☉), reveal clustered bursty star formation with halo-scale efficiencies of 10–30% in massive halos and surprisingly high efficiencies (≳1%) in some low-mass halos hosting ultra-compact galaxies, compare UV luminosity functions against observations from z∼9 to 25 finding broad agreement except a slight overprediction of bright galaxies, analyze mass-dependent UV variability, and introduce a simple Population III model consistent with independent predictions.
AI.motivation: The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an unexpected abundance and rapid growth of galaxies at cosmic dawn, challenging existing galaxy formation models. This motivates the need for new, high-resolution simulations to uncover the physical processes driving early galaxy assembly.
AI.method: The study uses the FIRE-3 model to run two suites of cosmological hydrodynamic simulations: BonFIRE (∼40 cMpc box, baryon mass resolution ∼5×10⁴ M☉) for large statistics, and CampFIRE (∼5 cMpc box, run at both ∼800 M☉ and ∼6×10³ M☉ baryon mass resolution) for ultra-high resolution. A resampling procedure statistically combines both simulations to robustly predict galaxy properties across a wide dynamic range. A simple Population III model with a top-heavy IMF is also implemented.
AI.result: Galaxy formation emerges as clustered, bursty star formation. Halo-scale star formation efficiencies reach 10–30% in high-mass halos, while a subset of low-mass halos also show surprisingly high efficiencies (≳1%) and host ultra-compact galaxies with narrow age spreads. Predicted UV luminosity functions at 9 ≲ z ≲ 25 broadly agree with JWST observations at MUV ≳ −19, with a faint-end turnover at MUV ≈ −14, but slightly overpredict brighter galaxies. UV variability is mass-dependent: halo-to-halo scatter dominates at low masses, while rapid temporal burstiness contributes comparably at Mhalo ≳ 10¹⁰ M☉. The Pop III model yields broad agreement with independent predictions and observational constraints.
AI.conclusion: The BonFIRE and CampFIRE simulations successfully reproduce many observed features of early galaxy populations, including the UV luminosity functions, and reveal key physical processes (bursty star formation, mass-dependent UV variability). The results help reconcile theory with JWST observations at cosmic dawn, and the Pop III model provides a consistent first step toward modeling the earliest stellar populations.

title: TRINITY: A coupled model of winds, radiation, and photoionised gas in molecular clouds. I. Methods and validation
summary: Multi-wavelength surveys place cloud dispersal at 1-5 Myr after massive stars emerge, before the first supernovae. Whether a cloud disperses, re-collapses, or leaks Lyman-continuum (LyC) photons depends on how pre-supernova winds, radiation pressure, and photoionised-gas pressure ($P_{\rm HII}$) couple to the shell. We introduce TRINITY, a 1D thin-shell code that succeeds WARPFIELD. TRINITY evolves the bubble-shell structure under winds, supernovae, direct and dust-reprocessed radiation pressure, $P_{\rm HII}$, and gravity. A phase-aware prescription drives the shell with the larger of the hot-bubble and photoionised pressures when energy-driven, and $P_{\rm HII}$ plus ram pressure when momentum-driven. The initial cloud may be uniform, a piecewise power law, or a Bonnor-Ebert sphere; shell structure, hot-bubble cooling, photon absorption, and LyC escape evolve with the dynamics. We validate against analytic wind and photoionisation limits and survey clouds of mass $10^5$-$10^{6.5}\,M_\odot$, core density $10^3$-$10^4$ cm$^{-3}$, and star-formation efficiency $\varepsilon=0.01$-$0.30$. $P_{\rm HII}$ enlarges the shell radius by roughly 17% at 10 Myr in the fiducial run. At higher efficiency, the energy-driven phase lasts under 1 Myr, radiation pressure stays sub-dominant, and $P_{\rm HII}$ remains dynamically important in the momentum-driven phase. Cloud structure sets both phase durations and outcomes: at fixed mass, core density, and efficiency, homogeneous and shallow clouds re-collapse while a steep $ρ\propto r^{-2}$ cloud keeps expanding, and Bonnor-Ebert clouds disperse roughly 55% later than homogeneous ones. Thus $P_{\rm HII}$ and cloud structure both shape feedback-driven expansion even when the stellar population is fixed. TRINITY is an efficient, interpretable framework to map feedback dominance across cloud parameter space and resolved H II regions.

AI.tldr: TRINITY, a 1D thin-shell code, models how winds, supernovae, radiation pressure, and photoionised-gas pressure drive cloud dispersal, finding that photoionisation pressure and cloud structure significantly affect shell expansion and cloud fate.
AI.motivation: To understand how pre-supernova feedback mechanisms (winds, radiation pressure, photoionised-gas pressure) determine whether a molecular cloud disperses, re-collapses, or leaks Lyman-continuum photons before the first supernovae.
AI.method: Developed TRINITY, a 1D thin-shell code that evolves bubble-shell structure under winds, supernovae, direct/dust-reprocessed radiation pressure, photoionised-gas pressure, and gravity, using a phase-aware prescription that switches between energy-driven and momentum-driven regimes.
AI.result: Photoionised pressure enlarges shell radius by ~17% at 10 Myr. At higher star-formation efficiency, energy-driven phase lasts <1 Myr; radiation pressure stays sub-dominant; photoionised pressure dominates in momentum-driven phase. Cloud structure determines outcomes: homogeneous/shallow clouds re-collapse, steep ρ∝r^{-2} clouds expand, Bonnor-Ebert clouds disperse ~55% later than homogeneous ones.
AI.conclusion: Both photoionised-gas pressure and cloud internal structure significantly shape feedback-driven cloud expansion independently of the stellar population, and TRINITY provides an efficient framework to map feedback dominance across cloud parameter space.

title: Transient axion streams from disrupted miniclusters
summary: We investigate the formation and evolution of axion streams generated by the tidal disruption of axion miniclusters through stellar encounters in the Milky Way halo. Combining a large-scale Monte Carlo treatment of repeated stellar flybys with a tracer reconstruction of the stripped debris, we follow the phase-space evolution of the streams across a broad range of galactocentric radii and assess their contribution to the local dark matter distribution. We find that the kinetic energy of the stripped debris typically exceeds its residual self-gravitational binding energy at formation, so that the subsequent evolution is dominated by anisotropic free expansion and orbital shear. As a result, stream densities can decrease by factors as large as $\sim10^{-9}$ over Galactic timescales, strongly suppressing the steady-state abundance of dense streams near the Solar circle. At the Solar radius, only a small fraction of realizations yields a nonzero encounter probability over a 10 year exposure, implying that observable streams are dominated by rare recent and nearby disruption events rather than by a persistent population of long-lived overdense substructure. Despite this rapid dilution, the streams remain dynamically cold and produce detector-frame linewidths many orders of magnitude narrower than the cavity bandwidths of current haloscope experiments. For representative haloscope configurations, we find characteristic stream linewidths in the range $Δν_{\rm stream}\sim10^{-7}-10^{1}\,{\rm Hz}$, while the corresponding Doppler drift remains well below the cavity response width.

AI.tldr: This paper studies axion streams from tidal disruption of miniclusters by stellar encounters in the Milky Way, finding that streams rapidly dilute (~10⁻⁹ density reduction) and are dominated by rare, recent events rather than persistent substructure, yet remain dynamically cold with extremely narrow linewidths (10⁻⁷–10¹ Hz) far below haloscope cavity bandwidths.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation, evolution, and detectability of axion streams generated by tidal stripping of axion miniclusters via stellar encounters in the Galactic halo, and to assess whether such streams constitute a viable source for direct axion detection experiments.
AI.method: Combines a large-scale Monte Carlo treatment of repeated stellar flybys with a tracer reconstruction of stripped debris to follow phase-space evolution of streams across a range of galactocentric radii.
AI.result: Stripped debris kinetic energy typically exceeds self-gravitational binding energy, leading to anisotropic free expansion and orbital shear. Stream densities decrease by up to ~10⁻⁹ over Galactic timescales, suppressing steady-state abundance near the Solar circle. Only a small fraction of realizations yields nonzero encounter probability over 10 years at Solar radius. Stream linewidths range Δν_stream ~ 10⁻⁷–10¹ Hz, with Doppler drift well below cavity response width.
AI.conclusion: Observable axion streams are dominated by rare, recent, and nearby disruption events rather than a persistent population of long-lived dense substructure. Despite rapid dilution, streams remain dynamically cold and produce extremely narrow linewidths, far narrower than current haloscope cavity bandwidths.

title: MAGAZ3NE: Spatially Resolved Ages and Chemical Abundances of Ultra-Massive Quiescent Galaxies at z $\sim$ 3.5 using JWST/NIRSpec IFU
summary: We present spatially-resolved measurements of stellar age, [Fe/H], and [$α$/Fe] in three ultra-massive ($\rm{log(M_{\ast}/M_{\odot})>11}$), compact ($\rm{R_e} \lesssim 2$ kpc) quiescent galaxies at $z\sim3.5$ using JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy. These observations provide the first spatially-resolved constraints on $α$-enhancement at this epoch, enabling a direct test of quenching mechanisms before late-time assembly processes such as mergers can erase chemical signatures. The central regions of all three galaxies show both uniformly young ages ($\approx0.6-0.7$ Gyr) and elevated [$α$/Fe] ($\approx0.2-0.5$), indicating rapid, enhanced star formation shortly before recent quenching. Beyond the cores, two galaxies display positive age gradients and negative [$α$/Fe] gradients, consistent with rapid merger-driven quenching, while the third shows a flat age profile indicative of uniform quenching. The [Fe/H] gradients are also consistent with these trends, though we note that the metallicities reported by codes using $α$-enhanced models differ significantly ($\approx0.2-0.4$ dex) from those reported using solar-scaled templates. These data demonstrate that quenching pathways are diverse by $z\sim3.5$, with rapid, merger-driven quenching already operating in a subset of massive quiescent galaxies in the first two billion years of cosmic time. Furthermore, these results establish that explicit treatment of $α$-enhancement is essential for interpreting the star-formation histories of the earliest quenched systems.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy of three ultra-massive (log M* > 11), compact (Re ≲ 2 kpc) quiescent galaxies at z~3.5 reveals diverse quenching pathways. Central regions show uniformly young ages (~0.6-0.7 Gyr) and elevated [α/Fe] (~0.2-0.5), indicating rapid star formation before recent quenching. Two galaxies exhibit gradients consistent with merger-driven quenching, while one shows uniform quenching. α-enhanced vs. solar-scaled templates yield metallicity differences of ~0.2-0.4 dex.
AI.motivation: To test quenching mechanisms at high redshift before late-time assembly processes (e.g., mergers) erase chemical signatures, using the first spatially-resolved α-enhancement constraints at z~3.5.
AI.method: Spatially-resolved stellar population analysis (age, [Fe/H], [α/Fe]) using JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy of three ultra-massive, compact quiescent galaxies at z~3.5.
AI.result: All three galaxies show young central ages (0.6-0.7 Gyr) and elevated [α/Fe] (0.2-0.5). Two galaxies show positive age and negative [α/Fe] gradients (merger-driven quenching); one shows flat age profile (uniform quenching). Metallicity estimates differ by 0.2-0.4 dex between α-enhanced and solar-scaled templates.
AI.conclusion: Quenching pathways are diverse by z~3.5; rapid merger-driven quenching operates in some massive quiescent galaxies within the first two billion years. Explicit treatment of α-enhancement is essential for interpreting star-formation histories of early quenched systems.

title: Isochrone Fitting of Galactic Globular Clusters -- VIII. Homogeneous estimates of parameters for 27 clusters
comment: 35 pages, 18 figures, accepted to be published in Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We use the Stetson, HST, and Gaia DR3 data sets for 22 Galactic globular clusters to select their members and fit their CMDs with isochrones from DSED and BaSTI for $[α/$Fe$]=+0.4$ and an adopted helium mass fraction $Y$. As a result, we estimate the metallicity [Fe/H], age, distance from the Sun, and reddening E(B-V) for these clusters. Special attention is paid to identify variable stars among the cluster members. We combine these results with our earlier estimates for five other clusters into a homogeneous set of parameters for 27 clusters and investigate relationships among these parameters and their statistical properties. In particular, we count the giants on the red (RGB), horizontal (HB), and asymptotic branches using the clean data sets cross-identified to cover the entire cluster fields and count each giant only ones. This allows us to calculate the $R$-parameter, the ratio between the numbers of the HB and RGB, with unprecedented accuracy and to examine its relations with other parameters. These relations are much stronger for accreted clusters rejecting a constant $R$ value for them, possibly because of their heterogeneous origins and environments. For all in-situ clusters, a constant value of $R=1.31^{+0.06}_{-0.05}$ is consistent with the data. According to previous calculations, this value may imply anomalous energy losses in HB stars corresponding to an axion--photon coupling of $g_{aγ}=(0.66^{+0.11}_{-0.13})\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$. However, the observed dependencies of $R$ on cluster parameters require improved statistics and a theoretical understanding of these dependencies. By comparing $R$-parameter estimates from HST and Gaia in cluster centres and peripheries, respectively, we suggest that the peripheral HB population is depleted by about half when the cluster crosses the Galactic disk, then the HB recovers over 60-80 Myr.

AI.tldr: Using photometric data from Stetson, HST, and Gaia DR3 for 22 Galactic globular clusters, the authors select members, fit isochrones, and estimate metallicity, age, distance, and reddening. By combining with 5 earlier clusters (27 total), they compute the R-parameter (HB/RGB ratio) with high precision. Accreted clusters show strong R-parameter dependencies rejecting a constant value, while in-situ clusters yield R = 1.31, implying possible axion-photon coupling. Peripheral HB populations appear depleted by ~half during Galactic disk crossings, recovering over 60-80 Myr.
AI.motivation: To homogeneously characterize 27 Galactic globular clusters, derive precise R-parameters, and investigate their correlations with cluster parameters to probe stellar evolution physics and possible new physics (axions).
AI.method: Use Stetson, HST, Gaia DR3 data for 22 clusters; fit CMDs with DSED and BaSTI isochrones ([α/Fe]=+0.4, adopted Y); estimate [Fe/H], age, distance, E(B-V); identify variable stars; count RGB, HB, and AGB giants; compute R-parameter with cross-identified clean data covering entire fields.
AI.result: Accreted clusters show strong R-parameter dependencies rejecting constant R; in-situ clusters consistent with R = 1.31^{+0.06}_{-0.05}, implying axion-photon coupling g_{aγ} = (0.66^{+0.11}_{-0.13})×10^{-10} GeV^{-1}; peripheral HB depletion by ~half during Galactic disk crossing with 60-80 Myr recovery.
AI.conclusion: The R-parameter varies significantly for accreted clusters (heterogeneous origins) but is constant for in-situ clusters, with possible implications for axion physics. Disk crossing depletes peripheral HB stars transiently. Improved statistics and theoretical understanding of R dependencies are needed.

title: The Celestial Reference Frame at K Band: The CRF-K-2025 Catalog
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. To be published in the Astronomical Journal
summary: We present an updated K band (24 GHz) celestial reference frame (CRF) constructed from 3.5 million Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations collected during 211 observing epochs between May 2002 and December 2025 using the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), the HARTRAO-HOBART26 baseline, the HARTRAO-YEBES40M baseline, and the Korean VLBI Network (KVN) augmented with several other VLBI stations. We have successfully observed and determined precise angular coordinates for 1317 compact extragalactic radio sources, essentially quasars, covering the full sky. This updated K band catalog is designated as CRF-K-2025. The precision of CRF-K-2025 is characterized by median scaled uncertainties of 60 and 104 micro-arc-seconds in right ascension and declination, respectively. The increase in number of observations and sensitivity over earlier K band campaigns has resulted in a catalog with 493 additional sources and a precision approximately 25% better than the ICRF3-K catalog, and similar to the ICRF3-SX catalog. At K band, these quasar radio sources generally show less extended emission than at lower frequencies and thus can potentially provide a more stable long term celestial reference frame than at the standard S/X (2.3/8.4 GHz) observing bands of ICRF3-SX.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CRF-K-2025, an updated K-band (24 GHz) celestial reference frame built from 3.5 million VLBI observations (2002-2025) of 1317 quasars, offering ~25% better precision than ICRF3-K and median uncertainties of 60-104 µas in RA/dec, with potential for greater long-term stability than the standard S/X-band reference frames.
AI.motivation: To construct a more stable long-term celestial reference frame at K band (24 GHz) where quasars exhibit less extended emission compared to lower frequencies, while improving upon previous K-band catalogs in both source count and precision.
AI.method: Analysis of 3.5 million VLBI observations from 211 epochs (May 2002–December 2025) using the VLBA, HARTRAO-HOBART26, HARTRAO-YEBES40M, KVN, and other stations to determine precise angular coordinates for 1317 compact extragalactic radio sources.
AI.result: CRF-K-2025 catalog contains 1317 sources (493 more than earlier campaigns), with median scaled uncertainties of 60 µas in RA and 104 µas in dec, achieving ~25% better precision than ICRF3-K and comparable precision to ICRF3-SX.
AI.conclusion: K-band observations at 24 GHz offer a promising path to a more stable celestial reference frame than traditional S/X bands due to reduced extended emission in quasar sources.

title: Bar-driven gas redistribution suppresses star formation in spiral galaxies: Evidence from dust lanes in NGC 3351
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A Letter to the Editor
summary: We present observational evidence, based on high-resolution imaging from HST, ALMA, and AstroSat/UVIT, that the redistribution of gas driven by the bar in the face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3351 results in suppressed star formation in its central regions. Dust and molecular gas coexist in galaxies, allowing dust lanes observed in galaxies to be used to probe the distribution of gas. In the central regions of NGC 3351, covered by the stellar bar, dust lanes are visible in the HST F438W-F814W color map, but surprisingly, these areas lack molecular gas and recent star formation. The inward orientation of the dust lane morphology towards the galaxy's center suggests that molecular gas may have once been present in this region, but was redistributed to the center due to the stellar bar's action. The direction of dust lanes, therefore, indicates the past inflows of gas toward the galaxy center, with their morphology consistently oriented inward along the bar. These findings support a scenario where the stellar bar has efficiently channeled molecular gas into the nucleus, building the central reservoir while suppressing star formation along the bar.

AI.tldr: Using HST, ALMA, and AstroSat/UVIT imaging of NGC 3351, the authors show that dust lanes along the stellar bar trace past gas inflows that have redistributed molecular gas to the nucleus, suppressing star formation in the bar region while building a central gas reservoir.
AI.motivation: To understand how stellar bars redistribute gas in galaxies and whether dust lanes can serve as tracers of past gas inflows that affect star formation in bar-driven central regions.
AI.method: High-resolution multi-wavelength imaging (HST, ALMA, AstroSat/UVIT) was used to construct color maps (F438W-F814W) of NGC 3351, comparing dust lane morphology with molecular gas distribution and star formation tracers.
AI.result: Dust lanes in the bar region are visible but lack molecular gas and recent star formation; their inward-oriented morphology indicates past gas inflows that have already moved gas to the center.
AI.conclusion: Stellar bars efficiently channel molecular gas toward the nucleus, suppressing star formation along the bar while building the central gas reservoir; dust lane orientation serves as a fossil record of past bar-driven gas transport.

title: Double Dots: Compact Pairs Mark Little Red Dots and High-Redshift Broad-line AGNs
comment: 10 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome!
summary: We utilize JWST imaging of the massive lensing cluster field A2744 to find close pairs of compact sources with separations less than 0.25". A large fraction of these "Double Dots" correspond to Little Red Dots (LRDs) or high-redshift broad-line active galactic nuclei (BLAGNs). Our analysis of 31 identified pairs reveals a median separation of 0.15". Statistical comparison against a uniform background shows that these are mostly physical pairs. We find that at least 16 of the 24 previously published LRDs in this field (~67%) are such pairs, as are both of the high-redshift BLAGNs. We demonstrate that the presence of a companion can significantly contaminate the measured spectral energy distribution, potentially masking the characteristic ``v-shape" used for LRD classification. Furthermore, our 2D spectroscopic analysis of several pairs reveals that BLAGN activity is not confined to the redder member of the pair but can originate in either one. Since most LRDs contain broad emission lines, our findings suggest that close pairs are extremely effective markers of galaxies with broad lines at high redshift. We speculate on possible mechanisms, concluding that we are likely seeing merger-driven accretion.

AI.tldr: JWST imaging of A2744 reveals that ~67% of Little Red Dots (LRDs) and high-redshift BLAGNs are actually close pairs (0.15" median separation) of compact sources, where companion contamination can mask characteristic LRD spectral features, and BLAGN activity can originate in either component, suggesting merger-driven accretion.
AI.motivation: To investigate the nature of close pairs of compact sources ("Double Dots") in JWST imaging, particularly their relation to Little Red Dots (LRDs) and high-redshift broad-line AGNs, and to understand how binarity affects their observed properties and classification.
AI.method: JWST imaging of lensing cluster A2744; identification of close pairs with separations <0.25"; statistical comparison against uniform background to assess physical versus chance pairs; SED analysis to evaluate contamination effects; 2D spectroscopy of selected pairs.
AI.result: 31 pairs identified with median separation 0.15"; at least 16/24 (67%) previously published LRDs are such pairs; both high-redshift BLAGNs are pairs; companion contamination can mask the characteristic "v-shape" SED used for LRD classification; BLAGN activity can originate in either component, not exclusively the redder one.
AI.conclusion: Close pairs are highly effective markers of galaxies with broad lines at high redshift; the findings suggest merger-driven accretion as the likely mechanism behind these systems.

title: cBHBd: A fast code for the evolution of tidally limited star clusters and their binary black hole mergers
summary:
The evolution of star clusters is driven by stellar mass loss, two-body relaxation, and evaporation in the Galactic tidal field. Fast modeling tools are crucial for exploring diverse initial conditions and predicting cluster populations and their contribution to gravitational wave (GW) sources over cosmic timescales.
  We present an improved version of the clusterBHBdynamics (cBHBd) code, designed to evolve star clusters containing stars and stellar-mass black holes (BHs). We improve the treatment of evaporation in the Galactic tidal field and include the effects of metallicity and stellar mass functions. We also introduce new prescriptions for GW captures during BBH-BBH interactions and between resonant interactions due to distant encounters that increase BBH eccentricities.
  The updated cBHBd is validated against Cluster Monte Carlo (CMC) models and $N$-body simulations spanning a range of cluster properties. Seven model parameters are fitted to the CMC results with nested sampling. With the best-fit values, the evolution of the cluster mass, half-mass radius, and BH population over 13 Gyr is reproduced to within $\sim10\%$. The new GW capture prescriptions allow cBHBd to reproduce BBH merger rates from CMC models of massive clusters ($\gtrsim10^5,M_\odot$) and direct $N$-body models of lower-mass clusters ($\lesssim10^5,M_\odot$) to within $\sim20\%$.
  The improved cBHBd provides a fast and flexible tool for large-scale star cluster studies. With a runtime of about one second per cluster, it enables applications such as searches for globular cluster initial conditions, stellar stream modeling, and GW population synthesis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an improved version of the cBHBd code for fast evolution of star clusters containing stars and stellar-mass black holes, incorporating better tidal evaporation, metallicity effects, and new gravitational wave capture prescriptions. Validated against CMC and N-body simulations, it reproduces cluster properties within ~10% and BBH merger rates within ~20%, with a runtime of ~1 second per cluster.
AI.motivation: Fast modeling tools are essential for exploring diverse initial conditions and predicting cluster populations and their contribution to gravitational wave sources over cosmic timescales.
AI.method: Improved the cBHBd code with enhanced treatment of evaporation in the Galactic tidal field, inclusion of metallicity and stellar mass functions, and new prescriptions for GW captures during BBH-BBH interactions and resonant interactions from distant encounters that increase BBH eccentricities. Seven model parameters were fitted to CMC results using nested sampling.
AI.result: The code reproduces cluster mass, half-mass radius, and BH population evolution over 13 Gyr to within ~10%, and BBH merger rates from CMC models of massive clusters and N-body models of lower-mass clusters to within ~20%.
AI.conclusion: The improved cBHBd provides a fast (~1 second per cluster) and flexible tool enabling large-scale studies such as globular cluster initial condition searches, stellar stream modeling, and GW population synthesis.

title: Spectroscopic metallicities and first α-element abundances of RR Lyrae stars in Baade's Window
comment: 18 pages, 15 figures. Accepted for publication by A&A
summary: RR Lyrae stars in the bulge have been reported to be associated with the spheroidal, relatively metal-poor component. They offer a way to trace this component with precise distances. While a few studies of RR Lyrae spectra with medium/high resolution are now available, none of them target stars in the Galactic bulge. We present here a spectroscopic determination of Fe and α-element abundances for RR Lyrae stars in the Galactic bulge, with the main goal of providing a benchmark to calibrate other metallicity indicators, appropriate for this specific stellar population. We analyzed FLAMES/GIRAFEE spectra of 78 RR Lyrae stars (60 ab-type and 18 c-type). We applied a full-spectrum fitting technique to obtain the spectroscopic metallicity and overall α-element abundance. Distances are derived by means of a period-luminosity-metallicity relation, and orbits are computed by combining the radial velocities derived here with the proper motions from DR3. Gaia The resulting metallicities peak at [Fe/H] _median = -1.34 +- 0.04 and -1.44 +- 0.08 dex for ab and c-types respectively. The majority of the bulge RR Lyrae are metal-poor stars with relatively high α-element abundances around [α/Fe] ~ 0.25 +- 0.03 dex. We used our spectroscopic measurements to test different methods for deriving metallicities based on photometry, which utilize Fourier parameters in the light curves of the RR Lyrae. The data suggest a possible correlation between the metallicity difference and the [α/Fe] ratio, which needs to be investigated further. There are some ab-type RR Lyrae that show metallicities higher than -1 dex and low [α/Fe] values. We studied these stars kinematically and found a difference between three stars with similar [α/Fe] values and the main group, indicating that they may be slightly younger and correspond to the disk population.

AI.tldr: This study presents the first spectroscopic determination of Fe and α-element abundances for 78 RR Lyrae stars in the Galactic bulge using FLAMES/GIRAFEE spectra. The stars are predominantly metal-poor ([Fe/H] median ~ -1.34 to -1.44 dex) with enhanced α-element abundances ([α/Fe] ~ 0.25 dex). The spectroscopic measurements are used to calibrate photometric metallicity indicators, and kinematic analysis reveals a small subset of metal-rich, low-[α/Fe] stars possibly belonging to the disk population.
AI.motivation: To provide the first spectroscopic metallicity and α-element abundance benchmark for RR Lyrae stars in the Galactic bulge, enabling calibration of photometric metallicity indicators for this specific stellar population and tracing the spheroidal, metal-poor component of the bulge.
AI.method: Full-spectrum fitting of FLAMES/GIRAFEE spectra for 78 RR Lyrae stars (60 ab-type, 18 c-type); distances from period-luminosity-metallicity relations; orbits from radial velocities combined with Gaia DR3 proper motions.
AI.result: Metallicity peaks at [Fe/H]_median = -1.34±0.04 (ab-type) and -1.44±0.08 dex (c-type); [α/Fe] ~ 0.25±0.03 dex; a subset of ab-type stars shows higher metallicity (>-1 dex) and low [α/Fe], kinematically distinct and possibly disk-related.
AI.conclusion: Bulge RR Lyrae are predominantly metal-poor with enhanced α-elements; photometric metallicity calibrations may be affected by [α/Fe]; a small disk-like population exists among bulge RR Lyrae stars.

title: Cluster-centric trends in bar size and pattern speed: the case of Abell 2199
comment: 14 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We investigate how the environment of a dynamically unrelaxed galaxy cluster influences the structure and dynamics of stellar bars. In particular, we examine cluster-centric variations in normalised bar size and bar pattern speed in Abell 2199. Our analysis is based on 578 spectroscopically confirmed members of Abell 2199, including a master sample of 325 galaxies with homogeneous stellar mass and star formation rate measurements. We identify 39 barred galaxies and measure their structural properties using isophotal ellipse fitting and three-component (bulge+disc+bar) photometric decompositions. For 22 barred galaxies with MaNGA integral-field spectroscopy, we estimate bar pattern speeds using the Tremaine-Weinberg method, obtaining robust measurements for 12 galaxies. Stellar population age and projected specific angular momentum are analysed using $D4000_{R_{\mathrm{e}}}$ and $λ_{R_{\mathrm{e}}}$ from the MaNGA Pipe3D catalogue. Abell2199 exhibits star formation-density and morphology-density relations despite its non-relaxed dynamical state. Early-type spiral (ETS) barred galaxies show systematic cluster-centric variations in normalised bar size, with relatively larger bars towards the cluster centre and smaller bars at intermediate radii. A corresponding variation in bar pattern speed with cluster-centric distance is also observed. These trends motivate a division at $\sim$0.5$R_{\mathrm{vir}}$, within which morphology-dependent environmental signatures become clearer, as barred galaxies in the inner region tend to host older stellar populations and lower projected angular momentum than those in the outskirts, with ETS+Bar galaxies retaining higher angular momentum compared to S0+Bar galaxies at comparable radii.

AI.tldr: This study examines how the cluster environment of Abell 2199 (a dynamically unrelaxed cluster) affects the structure and dynamics of stellar bars in 39 barred galaxies, finding that bars are systematically larger and slower in the inner cluster regions (<0.5 R_vir), where older stellar populations and lower angular momentum dominate.
AI.motivation: To understand how environmental processes in a dynamically unrelaxed galaxy cluster influence the size, pattern speed, and evolutionary state of stellar bars, which has been less explored in non-relaxed cluster settings.
AI.method: Analysis of 578 spectroscopically confirmed members of Abell 2199 with a master sample of 325 galaxies. Bar identification via isophotal ellipse fitting and three-component (bulge+disc+bar) photometric decompositions. Bar pattern speeds measured using the Tremaine-Weinberg method on MaNGA IFU data for 22 galaxies (robust for 12). Stellar ages and specific angular momentum from D4000_Re and λ_Re from MaNGA Pipe3D catalogue.
AI.result: Abell 2199 exhibits star formation-density and morphology-density relations despite its non-relaxed state. Early-type spiral (ETS) barred galaxies show larger normalized bars toward the cluster centre and smaller bars at intermediate radii, with corresponding variations in bar pattern speed. At <0.5 R_vir, barred galaxies host older stellar populations and lower projected angular momentum. ETS+Bar galaxies retain higher angular momentum than S0+Bar galaxies at comparable radii.
AI.conclusion: Cluster-centric environmental processes in even dynamically unrelaxed clusters systematically affect bar properties, with a clear transition at ~0.5 R_vir separating inner-region barred galaxies (older, slower bars, lower angular momentum) from outer-region ones, and morphology-dependent angular momentum differences persist at fixed radius.

title: Non-conservation and time non-locality of biased tracers
summary: We study the effect of ongoing formation and merger on the assumed number conservation of biased tracers. Using a Lagrangian approach we present a model of the number density which accounts for such effects. The model is nonlocal in time, reflecting the gradual assembly of tracers from the underlying matter. The loss of tracers through merger is modelled by an environmentally-dependent sink, such that the merger rate is proportional to the local number density (higher probability of an event in higher density regions). We derive from our model a formula for the linear bias of non-conserved tracers, showing that such tracers debias more rapidly than conserved ones. Over time the large-scale power becomes increasingly suppressed relative to the conserved prediction, behaviour which has been observed in simulations elsewhere. Implications for current modelling approaches are discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper models how ongoing formation and merging of biased tracers (e.g., galaxies, halos) violate number conservation, using a Lagrangian framework with a time-nonlocal and environment-dependent merger sink, finding that non-conserved tracers debias more rapidly and show suppressed large-scale power over time.
AI.motivation: To understand how the continuous formation and merging of biased tracers affects the assumption of number conservation, which is commonly used in cosmological bias models.
AI.method: A Lagrangian approach is used to model the number density of tracers, incorporating nonlocal-in-time effects (gradual assembly) and an environment-dependent sink term where merger rate is proportional to local number density.
AI.result: A formula for linear bias of non-conserved tracers is derived; such tracers debias more rapidly than conserved ones. Large-scale power becomes increasingly suppressed relative to conserved predictions, consistent with simulation results.
AI.conclusion: Non-conservation due to formation and merging significantly alters bias evolution and clustering, with implications for current modeling approaches.
